title: Phosphorus: allotropes of phosphorus (name only)
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — White, Red and Black

Phosphorus exists as allotropes named only (NEB scope): white (yellow), red, black (and violet/scarlett in older texts). Structure differences explain everything: reactivity, toxicity, storage, uses.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The allotropes (names only, with essentials)

| Allotrope | Appearance | Structure | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| **White (yellow) P** | waxy, white/yellow solid | discrete P₄ tetrahedra, 60° strained angles | very reactive; ignites in air at ~35 °C (stored under water); soluble in CS₂; poisonous (~0.1 g lethal); garlic odour; glows in dark (slow oxidation — chemiluminescence) |
| **Red P** | dark red powder | polymeric chains (P₄ tetrahedra opened and linked) | much less reactive; does not ignite spontaneously; insoluble in CS₂; non-poisonous; made by heating white P at 250–300 °C in inert atmosphere |
| **Black P** | black, flaky | layered (like graphite, corrugated sheets) | most stable; least reactive; conducts (semiconductor); made under high pressure |

### 2.2 Conversion chemistry

- White → red: heat 250–300 °C (inert atmosphere / with a trace of I₂ catalyst).
- Red → white: distil red P above 400 °C; vapour condenses as white P (P₄ re-forms).
- Allotropy is reversible through the vapour: the P₄ unit is the thermodynamic root.

### 2.3 Uses

- **White P:** matches (old "strike-anywhere"), rat poison, smoke screens (P burns to P₂O₅ fog), phosphor bronze.
- **Red P:** safety matches (on the box side), fireworks, semiconductors (InP), protection of metal surfaces.
- **Black P:** research/semiconductor (phosphorene layers).

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Allotropy** | Same element, different structural forms | white/red/black P |
| **P₄ tetrahedron** | Four P atoms at tetrahedral corners, 60° P–P–P | white phosphorus |
| **Chemiluminescence** | Light from a chemical reaction | white P glow |
| **Spontaneous ignition** | Ignition at ambient temperature | white P in air |
| **Safety match** | Red P on striking surface, oxidant on stick | red P + KClO₃ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why white phosphorus is so reactive

- The P₄ tetrahedron forces 60° angles on atoms whose bonding orbitals prefer ~90–109° — the bent bonds are strained, energy-rich, and desperate to react. Ignition at 35 °C follows; hence storage under water (cutting it under water too — it ignites on the knife).
- Red phosphorus polymerises those tetrahedra: strain released, reactivity tamed.

### 4.2 Why white P glows

- Slow oxidation at the surface gives excited P₄O₆/P₂O₃ fragments that emit light — chemiluminescence, the old "phosphorescence" that named the element (light-bearer). The glow is cold light: no flame.

### 4.3 Safety vs strike-anywhere matches

- **Safety match:** red P on the box, KClO₃ + antimony sulphide + glue on the stick head — friction ignites the red P/KClO₃ pair only at the box.
- **Strike-anywhere:** the oxidant and reducer both live in the head (P₄S₃ + KClO₃) — ignites on any rough surface. Red P's low reactivity makes the safety match possible.

## 5. Comparison Tables

| Property | White P | Red P |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | discrete P₄ tetrahedra | polymeric chains |
| Reactivity | very high (ignites 35 °C) | low |
| Toxicity | very poisonous | non-poisonous |
| Solubility | soluble in CS₂ | insoluble in CS₂ |
| Storage | under water | dry, safe |
| Glow | yes | no |
| Use | matches (old), rat poison | safety matches, fireworks |

## 6. Common Confusions

- **"Red phosphorus is red because of impurities."** The colour is structural — polymerised chains with different electronic structure, not dirt.
- **"White P is stored under kerosene."** Under **water** — it must be excluded from air; it is also insoluble in water, which kerosene is not guaranteed against.
- **"Black phosphorus is just dirty red."** Black P is the high-pressure, layered, semiconducting allotrope — the most stable form.

## 7. Exam Application

- Allotrope table with structure → property logic (strain story).
- Conversion conditions both ways (250–300 °C forward; >400 °C distillation back).
- Safety-match chemistry: which component sits where.

summary: Phosphorus wears three structural masks. **White P** — waxy, discrete P₄ tetrahedra whose 60° angles strain every bond — ignites at 35 °C, glows in the dark, dissolves in CS₂, poisons at 0.1 g, and lives under water; it fed the old strike-anywhere matches, rat poisons and smoke screens. **Red P** — the same atoms polymerised into strain-free chains (250–300 °C conversion) — is safe, non-poisonous, CS₂-insoluble, and powers the safety match's box side plus fireworks and InP chips. **Black P** — layered like graphite, made under pressure — is the most stable and semiconducting. Distil red P above 400 °C and the P₄ vapour re-condenses as white: allotropy reversible through the vapour. The lesson of the pair: strain is reactivity, and polymerising the strain buys safety.
